summaries.example: Imagine a row of cups slowly changing from very small to very large. Some cups are clearly small, and some are clearly not small. But one cup may be hard to classify. If we add only a tiny amount of water at a time, it is tempting to say that every cup stays small until the end. That reasoning leads to a puzzle: how can many tiny changes turn a small cup into a large one?
summaries.summary: Vagueness happens when a word has borderline cases. “Tall,” “old,” “child,” and “heap” often work this way. A person may be unsure because they need better information, but some philosophical cases seem difficult even in principle. This difference is called the difference between relative and absolute borderline cases. Vagueness is not the same as ambiguity, where one word has separate meanings, and it is not the same as generality, where a word covers many kinds of things. Vagueness creates the sorites paradox. If one grain cannot make a heap stop being a heap, and we repeat this for every grain, we seem forced to say that even one grain is a heap. Philosophers offer different solutions. Some use many truth-values between true and false. Supervaluationism says a borderline statement may lack a truth-value but that a larger statement can still be true under every reasonable way of making the meaning sharper. Subvaluationism allows a statement to be both true and false and uses a special logic to avoid every statement following from a contradiction. Contextualists say the meaning’s application can shift with conversation, interests, or other context. The entry also asks whether vagueness is only in language or can occur in thought, maps, music, and perhaps objects themselves.
key_ideas: Words such as “tall,” “old,” and “heap” can have borderline cases.
Sometimes more information could settle a question. In other cases, the problem may be in the idea or word itself.
Vagueness is different from ambiguity: an ambiguous word has different meanings, while a vague meaning has blurry edges.
Philosophers disagree about whether borderline statements are true, false, both, neither, or dependent on the situation.
Some theories use several degrees of truth, while others keep ordinary logic but allow gaps between true and false.
Vagueness may belong only to language, or it may also involve thoughts, pictures, music, or the world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Vague words are useful because they let us communicate without measuring everything exactly. But vagueness can also cause puzzles, disagreements, and problems in rules or laws. Studying it helps us ask what words mean, how logic works, and when uncertainty comes from missing information rather than from a word’s blurry boundaries.

important_terms.definition: A word or idea is vague when some cases are hard to place clearly into one group or another.
A case that does not seem clearly included or clearly excluded by a word or idea.
A puzzle made by saying that one tiny change cannot matter, then repeating that claim many times until it gives a silly result.
A word with more than one meaning, such as “bat,” which can name an animal or sports equipment.
Using a broad group name that includes many different things, such as “animal” including cats, birds, and fish.

questions_to_think_about: When does a pile of sand become a heap?
Can a word have a blurry edge but still be useful?
If one tiny change does not matter, do many tiny changes matter?
Should a borderline answer be called true, false, or something else?

summaries.example: Consider a sequence of people whose ages differ by one day. The first is clearly a child, while the last is clearly an adult. summaries.summary: The entry examines vagueness as the possession of borderline cases and treats inquiry resistance as a central diagnostic. A relative borderline case may become decidable through better evidence, whereas an absolute borderline case appears resistant to every possible method of settling the issue. This distinction separates vagueness from ordinary ignorance. Vagueness is also distinguished from ambiguity, which concerns multiple meanings, and generality, which concerns a term’s coverage of many kinds of things. The main logical challenge is the sorites paradox: a sequence of apparently harmless one-step transitions seems to preserve a vague predicate all the way from a clear positive to a clear negative. One response, epistemicism, retains classical logic and bivalence by positing a sharp threshold whose location is unknowable. Many-valued theories assign intermediate truth-values, though they face questions about compound statements and hedging. Supervaluationism treats borderline atomic statements as truth-value gaps while evaluating compounds across admissible precisifications; this preserves some classical-looking results but creates tensions about inference and truth. Subvaluationism instead allows truth-value gluts and requires a paraconsistent logic. Contextualists explain the paradox through shifts in the extension of a term as conversational standards, commitments, or interests change, though critics ask whether every sorites can generate such shifts. Kit Fine’s later holistic proposal argues that a series can be globally unstable without containing a particular case that is intrinsically indeterminate. Finally, the entry considers whether vagueness is only linguistic or can belong to thought, representation, music, and metaphysical reality.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes uncertainty caused by limited inquiry from indeterminacy that seems built into a question’s application.
Vagueness differs from ambiguity and generality, especially because new information about a borderline case can reduce confidence in a claim.
The sorites paradox pressures us either to reject a seemingly valid small-step principle or to revise classical assumptions about vagueness and logic.
Epistemicism keeps classical bivalence and proposes hidden sharp boundaries that we cannot know; rival approaches reject or reinterpret this picture.
Supervaluationism, subvaluationism, many-valued logic, and contextualism disagree about truth-values, contradiction, precision, and the role of context.
Kit Fine’s global approach challenges the idea that vagueness requires any particular locally borderline case, while the final section questions whether all vagueness is linguistic.
summaries.why_it_matters: Vagueness affects ordinary classification, scientific description, legal interpretation, and philosophical reasoning. It shows that useful language need not have perfectly sharp boundaries, but it also tests whether classical logic can describe everyday concepts. The competing theories clarify different possibilities: uncertainty, indeterminacy, contextual change, degrees of truth, gaps, gluts, or a more global form of unsettledness.

important_terms.definition: A predicate or concept is vague when it has cases that are not definitely within or definitely outside its application.
A case whose status cannot be settled by the relevant inquiry, at least in the strongest, absolute sense discussed in the entry.
A case that is unclear only because available tests, evidence, or methods of inquiry are limited.
A chain of apparently plausible small-step inferences that moves from a clear case to a clearly unacceptable conclusion.
The view that vague statements receive degrees of truth, often represented by values between full falsehood and full truth.
The view that a borderline statement may lack a truth-value, while a compound is true if it is true under every admissible sharpening of vague terms.
The view that application of a vague term can shift with context, conversational commitments, or interests.

questions_to_think_about: Does ignorance of a boundary differ philosophically from there being no boundary?
Can a theory preserve ordinary logical principles while denying truth-values to borderline sentences?
If context shifts the application of a term, can a sorites argument stabilize the context and still proceed?
Would a map, musical passage, or mental image be vague even if it is not linguistic?
Should a logical theory remain neutral about whether vague objects exist?

summaries.example: Suppose students line up from shortest to tallest. Everyone agrees that the first student is not tall and the last student is tall. If adding one millimeter never changes a student from not tall to tall, then repeating that thought seems to show that nobody in the line is tall. This is a version of the sorites paradox. The puzzle is not solved simply by saying “tall” is useful but general, because the question is why some students seem to be borderline tall.
summaries.summary: Vagueness concerns borderline cases: cases for which a term does not provide an obvious yes-or-no classification. The entry separates relative borderline cases, where improved evidence might settle the matter, from absolute cases that resist every possible inquiry. It compares vagueness with ambiguity and generality. An ambiguous term has distinct meanings; a general term applies to many items; a vague term has an uncertain boundary in one of its meanings. The central challenge is the sorites paradox. If a tiny change cannot turn a clear example into a nonexample, repeating that claim across a long series appears to preserve the original description too far. Philosophers respond in several ways. Epistemicists retain classical logic and say that vague predicates have exact thresholds, although we cannot know where they are. Many-valued logicians assign intermediate truth-values. Supervaluationists treat some borderline claims as lacking truth-values but assess them by considering acceptable ways of sharpening the language. Subvaluationists allow some claims to be both true and false and use a logic designed to prevent contradiction from making everything follow. Contextualists argue that standards can shift as a conversation, a speaker’s interests, or earlier commitments change. The entry also discusses higher-order vagueness, a debate over whether borderline status itself can be borderline, and Kit Fine’s proposal that vagueness may be global rather than located in one particular case. It closes by asking whether all vagueness is linguistic.
key_ideas: A question can be hard because we lack a good test, or because the concept itself seems not to settle the case.
Vagueness is not just having a broad category and is not the same as having several meanings.
The sorites paradox forces philosophers to examine whether every tiny change preserves a vague description.
Some philosophers keep classical logic and propose an unknown sharp boundary; others change how truth or context works.
Higher-order vagueness asks whether there can be borderline cases of being borderline, though some philosophers reject this idea.
The entry also asks whether vagueness belongs only to words or can occur in thoughts, pictures, music, or reality.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use vague language constantly: “nearby,” “expensive,” “late,” and “old” help us communicate quickly. Yet vague terms can create confusion in arguments and disagreement about rules. Philosophical theories of vagueness show different ways to understand that problem and teach us to distinguish unclear evidence from unclear concepts.

important_terms.definition: A word or idea is vague when it has unclear edges and some cases are neither clearly included nor clearly excluded.
An example that is difficult to classify because it is not clearly a member or nonmember of a category.
A chain of small changes that seems harmless one step at a time but ends in a conclusion that is clearly wrong.
A word or sentence that can be understood in more than one distinct way.
The feature of covering many things or kinds without necessarily having unclear boundaries.
A theory that says a borderline statement can lack a truth-value, while some larger statements are true under every acceptable precise interpretation.
A theory that explains changes in classification by shifts in conversational setting, interests, or standards.

questions_to_think_about: Is “almost ready” vague in the same way as “ready,” or does it merely add information?
If a better measuring tool settles a case, was the case vague or merely unknown?
Would several truth-values explain why “tall or average height” can sound acceptable?
Can a conversation change the standards for using a word without changing the word itself?
Could a picture or piece of music be vague even without making a clear statement?
